beats.say: The UK government owes nearly three trillion pounds. That's more than one hundred thousand pounds for every household in the country. So who exactly is it owed to? The answer might surprise you. A lot of it, in one way or another, is owed to ourselves.
In early twenty twenty six, UK public sector net debt was around two point eight seven trillion pounds, equal to roughly ninety three percent of the size of the whole economy.

vis.label: UK public sector net debt, early 2026

beats.say: Part one. How the government borrows.
When the government spends more than it raises in taxes, it has to borrow the difference. The gap each year is called the deficit. The total built up over time is the debt.

vis.text: Deficit: yearly gap. Debt: the total.

beats.say: Governments almost never pay off their debt completely. Instead, as old gilts are repaid, new ones are sold. What matters most is whether the debt is manageable compared with the size of the economy.

vis.text: Debt is rolled over, not paid off.

beats.say: Mostly, the government borrows by selling bonds called gilts. An investor pays, say, one hundred pounds for a gilt. The government pays them interest every year, then pays back the one hundred pounds on a set date.
Gilts are sold by an agency called the Debt Management Office. The name comes from old certificates that had gilded, or gold, edges.
Part two. Who holds the debt?

So who buys gilts? Roughly speaking, about a quarter to a third is held by overseas investors. A similar share has been held by the Bank of England. And around a quarter by UK pension funds and insurance companies.

Here's why it's partly owed to ourselves. Pension funds and insurers invest money on behalf of millions of ordinary people. If you have a workplace pension, some of your money may well be lent to the government through gilts.
Overseas investors include foreign central banks and big international funds. Their willingness to buy gilts helps keep borrowing costs down, but means the UK relies partly on foreign confidence.
Part three. The Bank of England.

The Bank of England became a huge holder of gilts through quantitative easing. After two thousand and eight, and during the pandemic, it created new money and used it to buy government bonds, to keep borrowing costs low.

vis.text: The central bank bought hundreds of billions.

beats.say: In recent years, the Bank has been reducing those holdings, a process called quantitative tightening. That means more gilts need to be bought by other investors.

vis.title: QE and QT
items: QE: Bank creates money, buys gilts

beats.say: Part four. The interest bill.
All that debt costs money. The UK now spends over one hundred billion pounds a year on debt interest. That's more than it spends on defence.

vis.label: in debt interest a year, projected

beats.say: The interest rate on new gilts, called the yield, rises and falls with markets. When yields rise, new borrowing becomes more expensive, and that cost feeds through over time as old debt is replaced.

vis.text: Higher yields mean higher future costs.

beats.say: About a quarter of UK government debt is index linked, meaning the payments rise with inflation. When inflation jumped in twenty twenty two, the interest bill shot up too.

vis.text: A quarter of the debt is linked to inflation.

beats.say: Part five. Is the debt a problem?

People disagree about how worried to be. Some argue the debt is too high, that interest costs crowd out spending on public services, and that borrowing costs could rise if investors lose confidence. Others argue that a country with its own currency and long dated debt can manage a high debt level, and that borrowing to invest can pay for itself.
The debt has grown a lot in recent decades. It jumped after the two thousand and eight crisis, and again during the pandemic, when the government spent hundreds of billions supporting the economy.

events: Debt around a third of GDP

beats.say: A reminder of how sensitive markets can be came in September twenty twenty two. After the mini budget, gilt prices fell sharply and borrowing costs jumped, and the Bank of England had to step in to calm the market.

vis.text: 2022 showed how sensitive markets can be.

beats.say: Part six. What it means for you.

The national debt affects you in a few ways. Higher interest bills can mean less money for public services or higher taxes. Gilt yields influence mortgage rates. And if you have a pension, you may own a small piece of the debt yourself.
So the national debt isn't one big loan from a foreign bank. It's millions of IOUs, held by pension funds, insurers, the central bank and investors at home and abroad. And quite possibly, by you.

vis.text: Millions of IOUs. Possibly including yours.
